title: Lambda Performance: Cold Starts, Concurrency & Memory
summary: Make Lambda fast and predictable: SnapStart, provisioned concurrency, memory sizing and streaming.
tldr: **Memory is the only CPU knob.** Raising memory adds vCPU and network share proportionally, so a CPU-bound function gets faster (and often no more expensive) with more memory.

Slow init on Java, Python or .NET → **SnapStart** (cheap, no code change). Strict, always-warm latency → **provisioned concurrency**, scheduled with **Application Auto Scaling** when traffic is predictable.
**Reserved concurrency** caps or guarantees a share of concurrency; it does **not** pre-warm anything. Long responses that should appear progressively → **response streaming**.

keyFacts.text: Memory range for a function. CPU scales with memory; at about **1,769 MB** a function gets the equivalent of one full vCPU.
Maximum timeout. Raising the timeout never makes code run faster; it only lets slow code keep running (and billing).
Configurable **ephemeral storage** (`/tmp`). Raise it for large scratch files instead of mounting EFS when you don't need shared or persistent storage.
**SnapStart** runtimes (Java 11+, Python 3.12+, .NET 8+). It works only on **published versions** or aliases, not `$LATEST`, and can't be combined with provisioned concurrency.
Default concurrent executions per account per Region (a soft quota shared by all functions). Reserved concurrency carves a fixed slice out of it.

comparisons.title: Compare: cold-start and concurrency controls
rows: SnapStart
Restores new environments from a snapshot of an initialized one
No extra charge on Java; caching and restore fees on Python/.NET
Long framework init on Java/Python/.NET, unpredictable traffic, no code change
Provisioned concurrency
Keeps N environments initialized at all times
Pay for every hour they're kept warm
Strict low latency; schedule it with Application Auto Scaling for business hours
Reserved concurrency
Caps the function and guarantees it that many slots
No extra charge
Protect a downstream API or DB, or stop one function starving others
More memory
Adds CPU and network share
Higher per-ms price, often shorter duration
CPU-bound work runs too long
Response streaming
Sends bytes as they're produced
Normal pricing
Long responses; cut time to first byte via function URL `RESPONSE_STREAM`

keywords.answer: Lambda SnapStart on a published version

keywords.cue: consistently low latency during business hours only
keywords.answer: Provisioned concurrency scheduled with Application Auto Scaling

keywords.cue: No space left on device, large file in /tmp
keywords.answer: Increase ephemeral storage up to 10,240 MB

simple sub-millisecond URL rewrite or redirect at the edge, cut cost
keywords.answer: CloudFront Functions on the viewer request event

traps: **Reserved concurrency** does not pre-initialize environments, so it does nothing for cold starts.
"Keep-warm" pings from EventBridge or a canary are a hack: they warm one environment, not the burst you actually get.
Provisioned concurrency sized for peak and left on 24/7 is the expensive answer when the question says "most cost-effective".
SnapStart and provisioned concurrency can't be used on the same function version; pick one.
Lambda@Edge runs only x86_64 Node.js or Python functions authored in us-east-1, with no VPC access, so "switch the edge function to arm64" is not a valid cost fix.
SnapStart also can't be combined with EFS or with more than 512 MB of ephemeral storage, so a function that needs EFS or a large `/tmp` has to use provisioned concurrency instead.
CloudFront Functions can't make network calls, so a per-request DynamoDB lookup at the edge needs **Lambda@Edge**, not a CloudFront Function.
